en: Advertising, in Dowbor's view, is not a moral problem of “bad content”, but the economic engine that governs the curation of the informational environment<1><2>199</2></1>. “A very important dimension is the basic logic of information systems financed by advertising: the return depends on maximizing engagement, attention, which leads the media in general, and social media in particular, to privilege the news that attracts most” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 30-31)</4>. When remuneration depends on screen time and advertising conversion, the recommendation architecture tends to reward what captures emotions and retains attention, articulating profiling, ranking and continuous modulation of the offer under criteria opaque to the user. The same rationality that organizes the individual consumption experience also reconfigures the public sphere under a structurally interested bias; for this reason, the “maximization of profit and dividends goes poorly with the dissemination of science and culture” <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 30- 31)</6>.

Under this paradigm, Dowbor elevates attention to the category of central economic resource because, in the digital regime, it acts simultaneously as raw material and commodity. It is captured, held and resold as measurable engagement, converted into advertising income and into power of influence. The diagnosis appears when the author describes the battle <1>p. 192</1> for people's attention time in the context of the predominance of the communication and information industry <2>Dowbor</2><3>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 25)</3> and, even more incisively, when he states that, caught in the web of the system, we pay at every step, both in costs and in the time of our attention <4>Dowbor</4><5>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</5>. The digital converts lifetime into an input of valorization, which makes the appropriation of that time inseparable from mechanisms of curation and choice design that maximize permanence and recurrence.

Thus, attention ceases to be mere passive “exposure” and becomes involuntary labor<1><2>200</2></1> that feeds metrics, profiling and, consequently, pricing. A capture that weighs, in the author's words, “on the pockets” and “on the head”, and which he describes as a subjective imprisonment inherent to this regime <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 30)</4>. In other words, the “information that platforms capture is free”, while “private information is appropriated free of charge” <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 66)</6>. Since this capture is carried out through governance, through interested curation, segmentation and persuasive interface architecture, consumer protection cannot be reduced to subsequent patrimonial restoration. The relevant harm may occur earlier, in the intelligibility of the offer and in the very shaping of the decision<7><8>201</8></7>.

The result, thus, is the so-called demand monopolies, in which it becomes necessary to use what others use, on pain of functional isolation<1><2>202</2></1> <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 24)</4>. The <5>p. 193</5> resulting compulsoriness combines with strategies of neutralizing competitors through acquisition and incorporation, reinforcing the concentration and planetary expansion of the dominant agent <6>Dowbor</6><7>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 24; p. 31)</7>.

It is for this reason that Dowbor refuses to describe these dynamics under the heading of markets in their classical sense. For the author, it is not a matter of competition to provide better services at better prices, since these structures charge what they want, from people and companies all over the planet <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</2>. The demand monopoly alters the competition regime. The dispute ceases to be organized primarily by the promise of better service at a better price<3><4>203</4></3> and comes to revolve around the control of technical standards, the imposition of compatibilities and the strategic blocking of exits. The replacement of WordPerfect by Word, when a specific standard became dominant, illustrates the conversion of voluntary adherence into operational necessity and, with it, the viability of arbitrary charging on a global scale, with macroeconomic effects that the author connects to inflation from monopoly profits (<5>profit-inflation</5>)<6><7>204</7></6> <8>Dowbor</8><9>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</9>.

This condition of inevitability thickens when the platform ceases to be merely a final service and comes to act as infrastructure for third parties, as critical support without which other economic activities cannot be carried out. Dowbor identifies in Amazon an expressive example of this transition, since, by converting internal tools into services rentable to other agents, the company transforms its dominance into the capacity to become <1>p. 194</1> a mandatory intermediary<2><3>205</3></2>, operating as an infrastructure rentier. In this design, economic strength does not reside only in the sale of goods, but in the control of intermediation layers of the digital ecosystem, sustained by structures of very high complexity and cost, difficult for new entrants to replicate and, for that reason, apt to stabilize value capture through recurring tolls. In this key, “infrastructure” ceases to be a figure of speech and becomes the material form of economic command in the digital environment, determining where circulation must effectively take place.

From this, infrastructure, already converted into unavoidable intermediation, assumes the function of a toll. The consumption of IOC comes to be lived as governed access, and the legal-technical enclosure that sustains this governance places back, from within, the discussion on the legitimacy of blocking and on which parameters may justify it at the level of consumer protection.

At the macroeconomic level, digital rentierism can be described as a regime in which the capture of surplus is stabilized less by the proportional production of goods and services and more by the administration of rights of passage over strategic circuits, financial, informational, logistical and legal, which become conditions of possibility of everyday life. The distributive consequence is the structural intensification of inequalities, insofar as income is realized as a repeated toll, through commissions, fees, interest, licenses and access blocks, while at the same time the asymmetry widens between agents who control infrastructures and users who merely circulate within them. In the scope adopted here<1><2>206</2></1>, this picture suffices to situate platform power as an informational and semiotic toll economy, <3>p. 195</3> in which access is governed and the circulation of signs is converted into a recurring unit of extraction.

The figure of the technofief reaches, with Dowbor, a sharper economic determination by situating the passage from industrial capitalism to a platform capitalism marked by digital rentierism. The axis of accumulation ceases to gravitate around profit derived from material production and shifts to the capture of flows<1><2>207</2></1> (of payment, of data, of decisions and of visibility) converted into value by the continuous measurement and modulation of circulation and behavior in a governed environment <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-31)</4>. At this stage, the platform no longer presents itself as a “producing company”, but as infrastructure of mandatory passage, apt to stabilize income through a toll on each movement and interaction carried out within the ecosystem.

At the level of digital business, this rentierism materializes as structured recurrence, in which the platform converts ordinary mediations of use into points of flow capture and stabilizes income through the governance of access. The empirical forms vary, but the common trait is the transformation of enjoyment into an architecture deliberately designed to enable the continuous extraction of value, shifting the IOC from the register of “content” to that of a functional arrangement of permissions and restrictions.

Dowbor treats the algorithm as the instrument of command par excellence, precisely because it operationalizes this grammar of tolls by articulating economic calculation and social modeling. The algorithm selects, orders and directs the experience with the explicit purpose of financial return, which authorizes reading rules of visibility (what appears to whom), of access (what requires authorization) and of conduction (incentives to purchase and loyalty) as the expression of a codified governance<1><2>208</2></1>.

<1>p. 196</1> This is a practical normativity inscribed in the technical architecture, in interfaces, permissions and compatibilities, which precedes and conditions the contract itself. By stating that to the rentierism that drains resources one must add the algorithmic control of people, the author makes explicit that algorithmic curation is not neutral. It operates as a device through which the extraction of value is converted into social control and subordinates even traditional companies to the logic of value to the shareholder, that is, to <2>shareholder value</2> <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 27-28)</4>.

The reason why this regime shows such resilience, in Dowbor's view, is also cognitive-institutional in nature. The mechanisms of extraction become progressively more complex and, for that reason, less understood <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3)</2>, causing financial-digital exploitation to remain “a nebulous reality”<3><4>209</4></3> for almost the entire population <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 13)</6>. This opacity is not merely technical, but political, insofar as the asymmetry of understanding disarms social resistance and postpones state regulation.

Dowbor makes explicit the gap between a digital economic base and still analog institutions by stating that the economic base has shifted and the institutions remain in the last century <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 8)</2>. He also observes that immaterial money allows sophisticated forms of exploitation that are difficult to understand <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 84)</4>. In this perspective, opacity operates as a technology of power that reduces contestation, hinders accountability and produces a field of regulatory impunity in which algorithmic control and rentier extraction reproduce themselves without proportional democratic counterweights.

In this architecture, the control of interfaces and signs ceases to be a marketing expedient and becomes infrastructure for value generation, regulating the visibility of what counts as opportunity and the very intelligibility of what counts as choice. It is <1>p. 197</1> precisely in this mediation by signs that the consumer's factual vulnerability (art. 4º, I, CDC) takes on its semiotic feature: one decides under a regime of representations and promises whose correspondence with actual delivery is structurally opaque and hardly auditable.

The analytical key lies in perceiving that such strategies do not operate as marketing “accessories” coupled to a core of enjoyment presupposed as stable, but as devices that constitute the Immaterial Object of Consumption (IOC) itself as an architecture of enjoyment. If, in the immaterial domain, the good is inseparable from what it does and how it does it, that is, from the actual experience that emerges from its technical organization and its mediation by signs, then the deliberate decomposition of that experience into toll points, such as access, progression, time and rarity, is not an external form of charging. It is the very form of production of enjoyment as an instrument of continuous extraction.

This rentier constitution of the IOC operates through the institutional conversion of technical abundance into administered scarcity. Contents and signs that could circulate widely come to be subjected to calibrated restrictions, windows and conditionings, so that the platform administers the very conditions of possibility of enjoyment in real time. What is delivered to the consumer becomes inseparable from the way in which delivery is conditioned, since income is realized as repeated charging for permanence, progression and circulation in the ecosystem.

The conversion of digital abundance into administered scarcity does not need “production” in the classical sense. The curation of access is enough. In a market of non-rival goods, rarity does not emerge as a natural limit, but as a decision of government, that is, as design and calendar that transform circulation into conditioned passage. Within the <1>Riot Games</1> ecosystem, rarefaction is not an accident. It appears as an operationally assumed and repeatable policy, which removes items from the ordinary flow of acquisition and returns them under selective windows, calibrating urgency, expectation and availability as economic variables.<2><3>210</3></2>

This rarefaction by government appears in at least two modalities operationally assumed by <1>Riot Games</1>. An expressive example lies in the so-called <3>Legacy</3> <2>skins</2>. They are presented as relatively rare not because of technical characteristics of the good, but because they “are not always available” in the store, reappearing intermittently in bundles, <4>p. 198</4> promotions and events <5>Riot Games</5><6>(Riot Games, 2025h)</6>.<7><8>211</8></7> The operation is typical of what Dowbor describes as a toll economy. The platform does not charge for the object as an isolated commodity, but for the turnstile of access to the catalog, that is, for control of the point of passage that decides when the good can be acquired and under what conditions. Digital abundance, which would allow permanent availability, is reconfigured into “scarcity by schedule”, converting time into price and access into income.

This same mechanism gains sophistication when scarcity is not only temporal, but also personalized. The “Your Shop” feature is not limited to offering discounts, since it acts as a segmentation device that transforms the history of use into a criterion of curation of what appears as opportunity. The official description itself states that the offers are produced by comparing the player's history with similar patterns, seeking to create offers that “you will like” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2023b)</2>.<3><4>212</4></3> What is organized, in practice, is a form of individualized toll. Access to the catalog does not present itself to the user as a stable and knowable set of alternatives, but as a variable showcase, built from inferences that the consumer neither audits nor reconstructs. In Dowborian terms, the algorithm ceases to be a mere instrument of convenience and comes to operate as an economic technology of command, because it decides which goods enter the zone of visibility and under which frictions and urgencies consumption becomes probable.

Administered scarcity, from this perspective, reveals that the “good” is less the isolated virtual item and more the access regime that surrounds it. By removing and reintroducing content through windows, by modulating what appears as an offer, and by conditioning the experience to proprietary cycles of availability, the ecosystem manufactures the bottleneck that sustains income. The content could circulate widely, but it is enclosed so that circulation is experienced as passing through turnstiles, with repeated charging of attention, permanence and payment. This design is not peripheral to enjoyment. It is enjoyment, in the sense that it organizes the experience <1>p. 199</1> as an economically governed path, in which the platform administers access to access itself.<2><3>213</3></2>

This regime of turnstiles is not merely a marketing policy. It is anticipated as the operating structure of the service, as if the instability of the catalog and of the conditions of enjoyment were part of the “product” itself, always redesignable in the name of updating, security and improvement. The contract makes explicit that the service may be updated and modified continuously, and that the company may, to the extent permitted by law, “modify, suspend or discontinue” any part of the services, as well as “restrict your access to any feature or part of the Services” and “remove or modify Game Content, including Virtual Products” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3><4>214</4></3> This type of clause is not a technical detail. It functions as a legal license to make abundance an administrable and, therefore, profitable field, because it allows the platform to convert what would be predictable into contingent, and what would be permanent into episodic, always under the argument of internal management of the ecosystem.

In this architecture, the so-called “Virtual Content” ceases to be a good “acquired” in the intuitive sense of the language of consumption and becomes a permission of access under private governance, subject to revision and, ultimately, to the very existence of the account. The same contractual section states that the account does not confer a “property right” on the user and describes Virtual Content as something that may be destroyed, deleted or modified within the services, including when the account is terminated or when the company makes reasonable and necessary changes<1><2>215</2></1> <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4>. It is here that the Dowborian tone finds its sharpest translation. When the supplier controls the catalog, controls time and controls the way access appears to the consumer, the economic center is not in the production of the item, but in the monopoly over the keys of the gate. Income arises from command over the conditions of <5>p. 200</5> passage, and passage is continuously recalibrated. Thus, the platform converts abundance into income, since, instead of selling a good, it sells passage, and transforms each reappearance, each showcase and each window into repeated charging for the right to cross its own turnstile.

Dowbor formulates the typical operation of rentierism in the digital economy as the political and institutional conversion of technical abundance into monetizable scarcity. The synthesis appears when he states that it is always a matter of transforming threatening abundance into a new form of scarcity <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 22)</2>. In this framework, abundance refers to the intrinsic reproducibility of the immaterial, while scarcity designates the socially constructed result of locks and fences that reinstate price and income. The change is profound because it marks the passage from an era of producers and buyers to an era of suppliers and users <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51)</4>, in which the central economic mechanism ceases to be the good and becomes the process. In this sense, today one owns a process and charges for its use<5><6>216</6></5> <7>Dowbor</7><8>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 52)</8>. The analytical consequence is that access becomes structurally revisable and conditional, administered as continuous permission and not as definitive transfer, opening space for unilateral reconfigurations of the rules of enjoyment.

From this standpoint, what is delivered to the consumer is inseparable from the way in which delivery is conditioned. It is deliberately that access is limited to contents, features and symbols that, from a technical point of view, could circulate in abundance, but are constrained to produce monetizable scarcity. The platform, therefore, does not merely alienate a good, since it administers the scarcity that it itself manufactured, continuously and revisably, converting access into conditional permission and reorganizing enjoyment as a permanently modulable process. It is this structural revisability, supported by legal-technical enclosures and by opaque criteria of modulation, that makes the extraction of income sustainable and, at the same time, legally sensitive. It intensifies the consumer's vulnerability and places the problem of the legitimacy of the enclosure back under tension as to practical verifiability.

Through the grammar of tolls, monetization strategies cease to be mere marketing accessories and come to compose the very functional substance of the Immaterial Object <1>p. 201</1> of Consumption (IOC). The platform institutes a field of choices and expectations mediated by signs, in which micro-drainage and algorithmic opacity deepen the consumer's factual vulnerability in its semiotic feature. As Dowbor suggests, the everyday governance of continuous services recalculates, in real time, parameters of cost, eligibility and access, causing the “product” to be lived as a regime of variable permissions, and not as a thing delivered once and for all. It is in this sense that the mismatch becomes evident of a dogmatics forged for stable material goods, when confronted with objects whose enjoyment depends on incessant modulations inscribed in the very technical and semiotic architecture of consumption.

When the consumption of IOCs is analyzed with categories designed for the purchase of corporeal goods, the operative core of supply is lost, because utility does not stabilize in a thing under the acquirer's dominion, but depends on external layers under the control<1><2>217</2></1> of the supplier, such as code updates, server maintenance, authentication, compatibilities and integrations. As a result, enjoyment is sustained by continuous technical-operational support and, consequently, unilateral changes in parameters of availability, compatibility or maintenance may degrade, reconfigure or extinguish the functional value delivered to the consumer, without this being reduced to mere contractual variation, since they bear directly on the practical conditions of delivery that make the experience possible over time <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40; p. 51-52)</4>.

In Dowbor's diagnosis, this governance rests on the supplier's infrastructural dominion, which concentrates “control of access codes” and “content management”<1><2>218</2></1> <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40)</4>. In this regime, the platform does not merely intermediate a consumer relationship; it institutes, through interfaces, rules and signs, the field of choices and <5>p. 202</5> expectations within which the decision is produced, which makes central the reading of the consumer's factual vulnerability in its semiotic feature.

The theoretically central form of “continuous change” consists in the fact that, in consumption based on repeated access, the conditions of use cease to be fixed and come to be renewed, modulated and charged recurrently <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>. Thus, when the economic object shifts from “good” to “process”, access becomes structurally conditional and revisable, administered as continuous permission<3><4>219</4></3>, which makes possible the unilateral reconfiguration of the rules of enjoyment <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</6>.

This same logic reappears, from a distributive angle, in the figure of “toll capitalism”, when Dowbor describes the shift of the economic center: if, in the twentieth century, the dispute gravitated around the ownership of the means of production, the decisive contemporary field reorganizes itself around the cost of access to information-dense processes and circuits, mediated by rights, licenses, patents and other barriers that enable charging<1><2>220</2></1>. In this regime, the monetization of the immaterial depends on an institutional engineering that converts technically cheap circulation into conditioned access, manufacturing scarcity and ensuring that knowledge is only realized as price when its diffusion is contained <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 22; p. 41; p. 51-52)</4>.

In immaterial objects of consumption, utility is not exhausted in the act of acquisition, since it depends on continuous decisions of support, updating and continuity under the supplier's control <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52; p. 57)</2>. For this reason, the legal problem is not the mere <3>p. 203</3> existence of variations over time, but the possibility that changes in the architecture of enjoyment reorder, opaquely, the level of utility actually delivered.

When the redesign of the immaterial object occurs without sufficient transparency for the consumer to understand, at least in material outline, the correspondence between what is presented in the offer and what is actually delivered, the change ceases to be perceived as a simple adjustment and comes to operate as an opacifying government of enjoyment. The platform can create structural dependence by making the experience progressively conditioned. At the same time, it can neutralize the capacity for contestation by keeping decision criteria, such as ranking, access, balancing or availability, under a black-box regime<1><2>221</2></1>. These are calculation procedures oriented to maximizing return and sustained by an algorithmic capillarity that the user cannot reconstruct by ordinary means <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</4>. At this intersection of administered scarcity, functional opacity and induced dependence, the terrain of the legal problem to be qualified below takes shape.

Dowbor formulates the idea of an inverted political sign to mark that the technical base of platforms does not carry a single purpose. The same infrastructure capable of expanding cooperation, circulation of knowledge and participation can be organized, through capture of incentives and through governance, for enclosure, extraction and government of the visible. The decisive point, therefore, is not “technology”, but the legal-institutional vector that structures access and defines whether technical abundance is converted into inclusion or into toll. For this reason, regulation is not reduced to an ex post patch; in network powers and infrastructural positions, it operates as structural design of continuity, quality, auditability and material transparency. In this scope, the problem can be formulated in consumer law language (CDC), above all with regard to the material shaping of the offer and of enjoyment in governed ecosystems<1><2>222</2></1>.

<1>p. 204</1> At the same time, Dowbor refuses to treat this systemic closure as an unavoidable technological fatality. The author records the historical possibility of breaking fences and proprietary standards, mentioning examples such as that of IBM and the migration to compatible clones, as well as the logic of open source (<2>open source</2>), which shifts the sale value without necessarily reducing the use value. Infrastructure thus reveals itself as a politically contestable field. The same technologies that today sustain oligopolies can have their political sign inverted and operate as tools of democratic connectivity, including through the guarantee of public and free access to the information highways, conceived more as streets than as toll instruments. The caveat is decisive to avoid a naturalizing reading of the demand monopoly, showing that the coercion of the technological standard does not stem from technical neutrality, but from a technique organized by specific regimes of property, governance and institutional design <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 39-40; p. 45; p. 56; p. 66; p. 88)</4>.

At the microeconomic level, Dowbor describes continuous reconfiguration as the capacity for dynamic and individualized adjustment of access conditions by information systems, that is, regimes in which essential parameters, such as cost, eligibility and terms, can be recalculated at every instant under proprietary criteria. In this register, he observes that the cost of credit is adjusted according to the bank's interests <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</2>. What is at stake is the replacement of relatively stable rules by an operational governance that transforms each user into a unit treatable by calculation, allowing access conditions to be continuously modulated by profiling, monitoring and automated decision, deepening the asymmetry between those who administer the system and those who submit to its material updates.

Informational asymmetry, from Dowbor's perspective, is not only a classic theme of political economy on the relationship between buyer and seller, but a systemic architecture in which platforms and intermediaries accumulate hypertrophied capacities to see and calculate, while users and the State itself remain in a state of cognitive blindness <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>. The example of the Serasa system makes explicit the expropriation of this power: “the Serasa system allows your bank account manager to have detailed information about your financial situation, and your cost of credit will be adjusted according to the bank's interests. And it was legalized” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</4>. This asymmetry becomes power of command because <5>p. 205</5> it enables discriminatory pricing<6><7>223</7></6>, understood as individualized modulation of price and conditions of the same service — and, in digital ecosystems, also of the conditions of access to and enjoyment of IOCs — based on inferences about profile, urgency and propensity to pay, operated by proprietary criteria and without comparable transparency <8>Dowbor</8><9>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</9>. By referring to Stiglitz as a reference for understanding these impacts, Dowbor inscribes the diagnosis in a consolidated tradition on informational asymmetry and inequality <10>Dowbor</10><11>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 48)</11>: in the digital environment, the ordinary capture of data from connected life radically amplifies this asymmetry and makes it structural, guiding economic decisions directed against the individuals themselves.

It is precisely at the convergence of administered scarcity, functional opacity and induced dependence that the terrain of the legal problem takes shape. The architecture can be governed to expand extraction, reordering the user's experience and straining expectations of continuity and predictability. The architecture of supply is not neutral: it incorporates its own ends of extraction, revealed in the way the service is continuously governed to expand income<1><2>224</2></1>, even at the cost of unbalancing the legitimately expected functional minimum. The social and regulatory effects highlighted by Dowbor, including as to the need for public containment of rentier dynamics and protection against the deepening of inequalities, make up the background for understanding that contemporary extraction depends on the governance of interfaces, data and signs as new material conditions of consumption. It is from this matrix that it becomes possible to describe, with <3>p. 206</3> precision, the architectural rationality of extraction that structures value capture in digital ecosystems.

This operational gear, stated here as a mechanism for converting abundance into conditioned access, reappears, under different lexicons, in four systemically linked cores. First, in the explanation that, in the economy of the immaterial, under rentier logic, business strategy tends to maximize the locking of access to produce monopoly effects <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 22-23)</2>. Second, in the formulation that knowledge only acquires sale value when its diffusion is prevented by legal and repressive apparatuses, producing artificial scarcity articulated with the idea of a “toll” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 41)</4>. Third, in the generalization of “toll capitalism”, in which access to processes and environments is enclosed to sustain permanent income <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</6>. Finally, at the infrastructural level, when the capacity of private operators to dictate who accesses the information highways through “communication corrals”<7><8>225</8></7> is discussed <9>Dowbor</9><10>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 49-50)</10>, that is, forms of closure that convert circulation into passage conditioned and administrable by a proprietary ecosystem. In terms of an inventory of analytical equivalents, artificial scarcity can be defined as the deliberate locking of access added to the construction of legal and contractual bottlenecks that ensure the capacity to charge for entry into the ecosystem. Once this inventory is fixed, it becomes possible to stabilize an operative vocabulary to describe contemporary rentierism as government of flows and accesses, and not as a mere form of “market”.

This closure worsens when the platform ceases to be merely a “final service” and assumes an infrastructural position for third parties, becoming critical support without which other economic activities do not operate. At this second level, power is no longer only that of the network, but that of the choke point. Whoever controls computing, distribution, means of payment, authentication or circulation of content comes to dictate access conditions and to carry out extraction through recurring tolls, sustained by costs and complexities difficult to replicate. Thus, the demand monopoly describes coercion by standard; infrastructure rentierism describes capture by unavoidable intermediation.

<1>p. 207</1> The materiality of command in platform capitalism is not located in a “good” delivered once and for all, but in the capacity to govern, in real time, the practical conditions of visibility, access and circulation that structure consumption itself. It is at this level that interfaces, data and signs cease to be mere marketing ornament and come to operate as decision-making infrastructure. It is defined what appears to whom, in what order, with which frictions, under which permissions, on what terms and at what rhythms. Rentier extraction is realized precisely because this architecture is modulable and asymmetric, allowing the supplier to retain metrics, logs and operating criteria, while the user sees only the effects on the screen and cannot reconstruct, by ordinary means, the link between capture, processing and result. Algorithmic governance, therefore, is not a neutral “technical means”, but the practical form by which the toll installs itself in everyday life, transforming the circulation of signs and permanence in the ecosystem into repeated units of monetization.

The informational toll economy translates, at the business level, into recurring forms of income that do not depend on “selling things”, but on organizing access and charging for the crossing. A first modality is capture by direct intermediation, with percentages, commissions and fees levied on transactions carried out within the ecosystem, converting the platform into a mandatory intermediary of the very economic encounters it hosts. The second is advertising and attentional income, sustained by continuous data collection and by hypersegmentation, in which attention time is captured, measured and converted into revenue through curation and choice design oriented to engagement.

The third modality includes income from access layers, when subscriptions, passes, expansions, time windows and recurrence mechanisms progressively shift relevant features and content to zones of additional payment, often combined with internal units of value<1><2>226</2></1> and proprietary circuits of credit and consumption, whose <3>p. 208</3> utility depends entirely on permanence in the environment. Finally, the fourth modality is legal-technical enclosure, in which Intellectual Property, license agreements and architectural restrictions operate as devices of authorization and blocking, multiplying points of permission and stabilizing the scarcity necessary for the immaterial to be realized as price and income.

This economic picture makes intelligible why, in platform-mediated consumption, traditional categories of consumer law need to be reread from the operational materiality of the immaterial. If extraction depends on governing access, visibility and permanence, the “product” is not reduced to isolated content, but presents itself as an architecture of enjoyment and permissions that structures utility over time.

For this reason, the relevant legal core shifts from mere price variation to the material intelligibility of the offer and to control of the practical conditions of delivery, since the supplier concentrates logs, metrics and modulation criteria, while the consumer perceives only the surface of the interface and its effects and cannot reconstruct the link between data capture, curation and impacts on utility. At this point, factual vulnerability (art. 4º, I, CDC) takes on its semiotic feature. The consumer decides on the basis of signs and promises whose correspondence with functional delivery remains structurally opaque and unilaterally reconfigurable, making the governance of access the decisive place where the practical predictability of enjoyment is organized — or disorganized.

In “Os desafios da revolução digital: libertar conhecimento para o bem comum”, Dowbor <1>(2024)</1> deepens this passage from industrial capitalism to a configuration dominated by digital rentierism, in which accumulation shifts from production to the extraction of income through control of intangible assets and intermediation infrastructures. The formulation dialogues directly with Varoufakis's reading <2>(2024)</2> on the consolidation of monopolistic structures in the digital environment and helps to anchor economically the thesis of technofeudalism, by emphasizing the capacity to capture vital flows and impose digital tolls on a planetary scale. <3>↩</3>

Dowbor uses “new mode of production” to designate an inflection in which the command of accumulation shifts from manufacturing to the control of informational infrastructures, intermediations and intangible assets, with the centrality of finance, data and platforms. The novelty is not to “digitize” the industrial, but to reorganize economic power through the governance of access and the capture of flows at scale. <1>↩</1>

Dowbor grounds “demand monopolies” in the specificity of the immaterial, which circulates on a planetary scale and with low territoriality, favoring accelerated concentrations: “the worlds of money, knowledge and communication [...] are, precisely, immaterial [...] they circulate [...] in planetary space, without the old ‘territoriality’” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 24)</2>. On this basis, the network effect converts standard into coercion: the utility of the system depends on the adherence of others, making the choice functionally compulsory; moreover, expansion is reinforced by the neutralization of competitors through acquisition or incorporation <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 24)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Dowbor condenses the transition to rentierism in the rupture between appropriation of surplus and productive contribution, fixing the criterion of proportionality: when “a minimum of proportionality between how much people contribute productively, and how much they get rich” is broken, the system ceases to operate as accumulation and comes to function as “unproductive rentierism”, that is, a “drain of social wealth” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 20)</2>. It is this logic — recurring capture by position and control of points of passage — that authorizes the characterization as a “toll economy”. In dialogue with contemporary typologies, Dowbor draws on Brett Christophers to group the main varieties of <3>rentierism</3> into seven sources: Financial, Natural resource reserves, Intellectual property, Digital platforms, Service contracts, Infrastructure and Land <4>Dowbor</4><5>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 20)</5>. <6>↩</6>

The distinction between profit and rent in Dowbor serves to locate the change in the axis of accumulation: profit tends to be linked to reinvestment and the expansion of productive capacity, while rent stabilizes as capture by position and intermediation — that is, gain derived from control of a “point of passage” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 5)</2>. This precision also has a linguistic dimension, since current usage blurs productive income and toll income, naturalizing the idea of “investment” for unproductive applications <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 20)</4>. Without eliminating the ambivalence, Dowbor observes that certain services may be useful and, even so, operate with disproportionate extraction typical of intermediation oligopolies, when the gain stems less from the productive contribution than from the inevitability of the crossing <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21)</6>. <7>↩</7>

The expression “unit treatable by calculation” condenses, in Dowbor, the reconfiguration of the user as an individual isolable and governable by inference, converted simultaneously into a source of information, risk and return, by virtue of algorithmic capillarity and the orientation toward financial maximization <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>. In this regime, the offer ceases to operate as a uniform standard and comes to admit continuous modulation (through frictions, permissions, advantages and limits) producing functionally differentiated deliveries under the appearance of an “equal” service, without the consumer being able to reconstitute, by ordinary means, the criteria of the variation <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</4>. It is this basis that gives intelligibility to the “directed instability” of the functional value promised in the consumption of IOCs. <5>↩</5>

The specific contribution of “micro-drainage” is not to reiterate that there is fractional extraction, but to make explicit its evidentiary effect: the intermediation chain is only intelligible to those who hold operational traces (logs, metrics, recommendation or ranking parameters, pricing and modulation criteria), so that the intermediary can reconstruct the link between data capture, profiling and automated decisions, while the user remains confined to the surface of the interface and to the perceived effects <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>. Thus, the legal problem shifts from “cost” to asymmetry in reconstructing the link and in practical verifiability. <3>↩</3>

The expression “mandatory intermediary” describes, in Dowbor, the passage from competition by product to competition by infrastructural position: rentier gain stabilizes when critical layers of circulation, computing and intermediation become unavoidable points of passage, shifting the dispute to the control of access. <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21; p. 31)</2>. The Amazon case illustrates this conversion of internal capacity into a generalized toll: “AWS as well as FBA are […] infrastructure rentiers.” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</4>. By building such layers for its own services and then renting them to third parties, the platform reorganizes the competitive field under structural dependence, since companies — including in adjacent markets — come to operate within conditions set by the holder of the layer. This position is sustained by technical and economic barriers to replication: “Amazon controls critical infrastructures […] in ways that it would be difficult for new interested parties (entrants) to replicate or try to confront with competition.” <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</6>. The relevant legal point is that intermediation ceases to be a mere “neutral” provision and comes to operate as unilateral governance of the point of passage, with effects on continuity, conditions of permanence and the power to impose recurring costs in dependent digital ecosystems. <7>Dowbor</7><8>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</8>. <9>↩</9>

Dowbor offers a systemic framework for contemporary rentierism by emphasizing the mismatch between the digital economic base and institutions still organized by categories of the previous period, which contributes to the persistence of extraction mechanisms that are hardly intelligible in the public sphere <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3; p. 8; p. 13)</2>. In the scope of this research, this observation is used only as a delimitation of framework, to situate platform power as an informational and semiotic toll economy — extraction founded on mandatory intermediation, governance of access and capture of the circulation of signs. <3>↩</3>

In Dowbor, the “capture of flows” designates the transformation of digital circulation into a continuous economic asset: payments, data, attention and decisions cease to be side effects of use and come to integrate a measurable and monetizable flow, whose extraction depends on retaining enjoyment within controlled layers (accounts, permissions, proprietary standards, terms of use and curation), reducing the possibility of relevant use outside the governed perimeter <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-31)</2>. The category reinforces that the consumption of IOC occurs as administered and continuously modulable access, and that the opacity of the functioning of this retention projects duties of transparency and loyalty onto the material shaping of the offer (CDC), especially when legal-technical fences (including IP ones) are coupled to the perimeter to stabilize capture <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 19-21; p. 28-31)</4>. <5>↩</5>

The notion of codified governance, in Dowbor's diagnosis, indicates that the central normativity of platforms is not exhausted in the contract, since it is materialized beforehand in the very technical architecture that defines the field of the possible, converting <1>design</1>, permissions and access rules into a practical regime of authorization and blocking. This command becomes capillary because “algorithms and artificial intelligence allow a capillarity that reaches every individual in the world” <2>Dowbor</2><3>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</3>, shifting “consent” to a function above all ratifying an arrangement already implemented, as can be glimpsed in the ordinary experience of compulsoriness: “I cannot move unless I am all the time authorizing some network to install cookies” <4>Dowbor</4><5>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</5>. In this key, the contract tends to operate as a subsequent discursive stabilization of a control already inscribed in the code, including in the administration of “access codes” and in “content management” as structuring dimensions of the platform <6>Dowbor</6><7>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40)</7>. At the dogmatic level, this primacy of technical architecture requalifies factual vulnerability as semiotic vulnerability: signs of choice (“accept”, “configure”, “personalize”) may conceal the material impossibility of bargaining and the insufficiency of auditability over criteria, limitations and effects of the system, reinforcing duties of information, transparency and loyalty in the shaping of the offer and of enjoyment (CDC). When this practical normativity is articulated with technical fences and exclusivity regimes, the closure of access must be read in light of internal limits of legitimacy, above all when the effective teleology of the design shifts to a regime of precarious and revocable toll over the enjoyment of IOCs <8>Dowbor</8><9>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21; p. 40)</9>. <10>↩</10>

According to Dowbor, the “nebulous reality” is not a spontaneous deficit of information, but an institutional effect of the growing complexity of contemporary mediations of surplus appropriation, which makes them less intelligible and, for that reason, less politicizable and attributable in common sense <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3; p. 13)</2>. The consequence is a practical blocking of collective response, associated with the picture of “institutional impotence”: “The institutional impotence we face leads us to a disastrous systemic disarticulation” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 8)</4>. At the same time, the author refuses to naturalize this opacity as a technical fatality and makes explicit its contestable character by stating: “This book is about making visible and understandable how the mechanisms work today” <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3)</6>. At the level of platform consumption, this nebulousness reinforces the insufficiency of merely formal transparency: the availability of terms, policies and documents does not eliminate the practical unintelligibility of the mechanism that organizes the capture and the toll embedded in the experience, which strains the reading of the duties of information, clarity and objective good faith in the CDC <7>Dowbor</7><8>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3; p. 13)</8>. <9>↩</9>

The contractual normalization of contingent availability and of the unilateral power of curation appears explicitly in Clause 4.5 of the Riot Games Terms of Service. The contract does not describe Virtual Content as the user's permanent stock, but as an object of continuous intervention by the supplier. Under the same clause, it makes explicit that virtual products “may (and probably will) evolve over time” and even admits a change in the “purchasing power of Game Currency”, giving as an example an increase in the number of coins needed to acquire “Virtual Products, such as skins” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. <3>↩</3>

In the official support material, the rarity of Legacy skins is described as the direct result of planned unavailability, and not as a natural trait of the good. The page states directly that “Legacy skins are relatively rare because they are not always available for purchase in the Store” and adds that, “from time to time”, they may be found “in bundles or in promotions during events” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025h)</2>. This formulation, in institutional language, materializes the transformation of digital abundance into administered scarcity, since the circulation policy is not a technical consequence, but a decision of catalog curation. <3>↩</3>

The logic of segmentation and personalization, which converts history of use into an economic criterion, appears clearly in the “Your Shop” FAQ. In answering why offers include rarely played champions, the material states that the system “uses your player history from the last six months to compare you to other players with similar patterns and create offers you will like” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2023b)</2>. The sentence is methodologically valuable because it does not depend on external inference: it assumes that the showcase is produced by analysis of history and by comparison, which supports the reading of personalized tolls as a form of government of access, operated under proprietary criteria of low auditability. <3>↩</3>

As an interface dictionary and bridge of references, the <1>Legacy Vault</1> entry synthesizes, in technical language, the idea of availability by windows. It describes the vault as a set of cosmetic content “only available [...] during special events”, including retired skins (“retired”) and seasonal content <2>League of Legends Wiki</2><3>(League of Legends Wiki, [202-?]d)</3>. The <4>Your Shop</4> entry, in turn, describes the feature as a periodic sale “personalized based on the player’s match history”, with six offers generated from the history of the last six months <5>League of Legends Wiki</5><6>(League of Legends Wiki, [202-?]o)</6>. These descriptions do not replace the official source, but they help name the mechanism and stabilize an operational vocabulary for the analysis. <7>↩</7>

The normalization of the continuous mutability of the service appears directly in Clause 10.2 of the Terms of Service, which reinforces the reading that administered scarcity is not an “event”, but a structural faculty, which transforms the predictability of access into a variable of management and monetization. <1>↩</1>

Clause 4.4 reinforces that there is no appropriation in the classical patrimonial sense, which supports the reading of enjoyment as a governed position and not as the consumer's dominion. The contract indicates that the account “does not grant you any property right over Virtual Content” and limits liability for “damages arising from the destruction, deletion or modification of any Virtual Content”, including “for any deletion of Virtual Content after the termination of the account” or for “reasonable and necessary” changes <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. At the economic level, this legal framing helps explain why the platform manages to operate the catalog as a toll, since access ceases to be something the consumer stabilizes and becomes something the supplier recalibrates. <3>↩</3>

The formula “owner of a process” is used by Dowbor to indicate that, in digital rentierism, capture ceases to depend on the alienation of a good and comes to stabilize through continued control of the conditions of use, converting enjoyment into authorized permanence within a governed circuit <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>. In this key, the relevant economic object is not a “content” in itself, but the very operation of access — its permissions, compatibilities and continuity criteria —, so that use becomes structurally conditional and subject to unilateral revisions <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</4>. The consequence is that the guarantees intuitively associated with acquisition lose practical density: availability, continuity and power of enjoyment come to depend on the holder of the infrastructure and on the private rules that administer the process <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</6>. <7>↩</7>

The architecture of access and enjoyment designates the set of technical-operational layers that sustain the utility of IOCs over time — code updates, authentication, server availability, compatibilities and integrations — and that, for that reason, shift consumption from the logic of the delivery (tradição) of a good to continuous participation in a governed process <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40; p. 51-52)</2>. In Dowbor, this mutation is described as the institutional passage from the regime of producers and buyers to that of suppliers and users and as the replacement of concrete property by recurring control of a process, in which economic capture is realized by charging for use <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</4>. Since enjoyment depends on these layers under the supplier's command, unilateral changes in parameters of maintenance, compatibility or access may reconfigure the functional value delivered to the consumer — by degradation, locking or discontinuity — without the phenomenon being adequately captured by the classical categories of acquisition and permanence of the good <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40; p. 51-52)</6>. <7>↩</7>

The reference to conditions of possibility aims only to clarify that the enjoyment of the immaterial depends on the supplier's infrastructural dominion over the practical regimes of access and circulation, so that the consumer's experience is structured by permissions and mediations controlled by the offeror — that is, by the administration of “access codes” and by “content management” as material dimensions of supply <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40)</2>. <3>↩</3>

For Dowbor, the rentier enjoyment of the digital tends to be organized as authorized permanence in a process: access is continuously conditionable and revisable by the holder of the infrastructure, instead of ending in the classical logic of delivery of a good <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>. This precariousness does not designate an episodic failure, but a functional trait of the arrangement, since the supplier preserves the capacity to restrict, reconfigure or end the experience through the administrative modulation of permissions, normalizing social life as a circuit of passage and recurring charging: “Living ceases to be a stroll […] to become a permanent race from toll to toll.” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51)</4>. At the limit, the very idea of access is refigured as governance by instituted scarcity, as the metaphor suggests: “Free access to the sea does not fill anyone's pockets. Let us close, then, the beaches. […] we become increasingly trapped in the race to increase our monthly income, without which we will be deprived of a series of essential services.” <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51)</6>. Within the scope of the CDC, this reinforces that signs of “service”, “plan” and “purchase” may mask a structurally revocable enjoyment, raising opacity and making it difficult, in practice, to anticipate and contest relevant changes in the conditions of use <7>Dowbor</7><8>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</8>. <9>↩</9>

According to Dowbor, the “barriers that allow charging” are not exhausted in technical locks or in licenses taken in isolation. The rentier capture of the immaterial stabilizes when the legal order reinforces the enclosure, including by repressive means, making circumvention of the locks an unlawful act. It is in this sense that the author describes the corporate hardening of control as a “strategy implemented through a series of new laws intended to extend the copyright term of the work, reinforce criminal penalties for infringing copyright, and to punish the use of technologies that tried to avoid the digital obstacles placed on digital content” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 42-43)</2>. The institutional effect is to convert the ordinary reproducibility of the digital into conditioned circulation: exclusion — through reinforced technical-legal fences — becomes a condition of possibility of the toll, that is, of the income extracted by control of access, and not by the social utility of diffusion <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 22; p. 41; p. 51-52)</4>. <5>↩</5>

The “black-box regime”, in the reading proposed from Dowbor, designates an institutional form of opacity in which relevant decisions are shifted to proprietary layers of calculation and organization — ranking, eligibility, visibility, balancing and availability — outside the user's ordinary intelligibility, in an environment marked by algorithmic capillarity and by the orientation of processing toward maximizing economic return <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>. The practical consequence is evidentiary and cognitive: the consumer has neither understandable traces nor a common language to reconstitute the effective criteria of modulation of the service, although they experience its effects directly in enjoyment <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</4>. In such a context, even when formal terms and documents are available, transparency may remain insufficient for control and attribution, since the relevant decision-making mechanism remains unintelligible — a point that is articulated with the diagnosis of complexification and opacity and with the insufficiency of merely formal transparency <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3; p. 13)</6>. <7>↩</7>

Dowbor formulates the “inverted political sign” as a thesis of institutional reversibility: the same technical base that today sustains drainage and enclosure can be organized for purposes of well-being and democratization, because the decisive vector is not “technology” in itself, but the arrangement of incentives and governance that structures access <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 82)</2>. The contrast appears when the author observes that, while technique makes cultural goods more accessible, “the laws […] evolve symmetrically to make access ever more difficult”, shifting the conflict to the legal-institutional discipline of enclosure <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 42)</4>. Hence the conclusion that the “right of access to knowledge” becomes an axis of economic democratization <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 65)</6>. This diagnosis finds a parallel in the treatment of network infrastructures and situations without effective competition, in which “private property and ‘economic freedom’, when there is no competition, lead to abuses”, that is, “it is private property, but not market”, with loss of public purpose <7>Dowbor</7><8>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31-32)</8>. The framework supports reading consumer law as bearing on the material shaping of the offer and of enjoyment in governed ecosystems, under requirements of transparency and loyalty compatible with the practical difficulty of reconciling profit and social objective in hybrid structures <9>Dowbor</9><10>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 87)</10>. <11>↩</11>

Discriminatory pricing, in Dowbor's diagnosis, stems from the capacity for individualization at scale. Instead of price and conditions presenting themselves as public and comparable attributes of the offer, they become variables calculable per user, modulated by behavioral and socioeconomic inferences oriented to maximizing return <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>. The Serasa example works as an institutionalized illustration of this rationality by recording that “your cost of credit will be adjusted according to the bank's interests”, showing that calibration may exploit asymmetries of information and estimated needs, and not merely reflect “risk” in a neutral sense <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</4>. The decisive legal point is not the existence of transparent segmentations, but silent differentiation that prevents the social comparability of price and hinders the evidentiary reconstruction of discrimination, since the criteria and data that sustain the modulation remain under the supplier's control. In this key, signs such as “personalization” may operate as an opaque technique of extraction, straining duties of material transparency and loyalty in the shaping of the offer and, when anchored in the exploitation of urgency or fragility, approaching the logic of manifestly excessive advantage (art. 39, V, CDC). As an internal parameter of control, open auditability and functional value equivalence apply here to make verifiable the logic of formation of price and conditions, as well as to allow judicial review of the dissociation between what is charged and what is delivered in IOCs. <5>↩</5>

In Dowbor's diagnosis, unproductive rentierism has a distributive expression when the link of proportionality between productive contribution and enrichment is broken, consolidating itself as a drain of social wealth in favor of rentier positions; this shift, for the author, marks the passage of the axis from capital accumulation to the logic of unproductive rentierism <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 13; p. 20)</2>. It is in this sense that the architecture of the service can be governed to expand extraction, shifting the axis from “gain” to the recurring toll embedded in the mediations. <3>↩</3>

The expression “communication corrals”, used by Dowbor, designates the infrastructural closure through which private operators come to control the conditions of access and circulation on the information highways themselves, consolidating the power to select, condition and administer enjoyment in proprietary environments <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 49-50)</2>. This closure is not reduced to a neutral technical option, because it involves the coordinated appropriation of layers ranging from “physical infrastructure” to “codes” and “content”, shifting the governance of informational space to private regimes of passage <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 49)</4>. In an economic key, the “corrals” operate as a condition of possibility of recurring charging for access and permanence, since they transform circulation into administered crossing and, therefore, compatible with the toll rationality that runs through the diagnosis of contemporary rentierism <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21; p. 49-50)</6>. <7>↩</7>

Internal units of value in closed digital ecosystems (points, proprietary “coins”, bundles and bonuses) operate as a technology of economic governance of consumption by shifting the user away from state currency and direct price comparison toward denominations defined unilaterally, with conversion tables and bundle sizes that may fragment the perception of spending and induce successive top-ups (recurring leftovers, partial recharges, conditioned bonuses). The design can be read as compatible with the logic of toll and repeated micro-extraction described by Dowbor, insofar as it brings payment closer to a regime of small continuous captures that are hardly salient to the individual <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29; p. 21)</2>. The relevant structural effect is economic entrapment: converted into an internal unit, the balance tends to lose general fungibility and to become a captive asset of the ecosystem, raising exit costs and making permanence a practical condition for not losing value already internalized. At the dogmatic level, this requalifies price as a semiotic component of the offer: signs of “promotion”, “advantage” and “ease” may conceal conversion frictions, circulation limits and redemption restrictions, straining duties of information, transparency and loyalty and, depending on the case, the prohibition of manifestly excessive advantage (art. 39, V, CDC). When this closed circuit is combined with technical and contractual restrictions on circulation, the governance of access by turnstiles and crossing costs is reinforced, the core of the diagnosis of toll and disproportionate extraction <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21; p. 39)</4>. <5>↩</5>

In Dowbor, behavioral influence stems from the economic design of advertising-financed systems: if revenue depends on maximizing engagement and attention time, curation and recommendation mechanisms tend to privilege what retains the user, making the informational architecture a direct function of profitability <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 30-31)</2>. The critique, therefore, is not directed at “isolated contents”, but at the regime of incentives that organizes visibilities and priorities in the communicational environment. At the dogmatic level, the sensitive point is the opacity of the ordering criteria: signs such as “relevance”, “trends” and “personalization” may conceal rankings oriented by engagement metrics and advertising return, straining duties of transparency and loyalty in the governance of the user's informational experience <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 30- 31)</4>. <5>↩</5>

The notion of “involuntary labor” gains precision in Dowbor when it is recognized that the platform does not merely offer an environment, but organizes an architecture of capture in which interaction itself is converted into an economic input. The material presupposition is individualization at scale: “8 billion people […] become isolable individuals, sources of information” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</2>. In this key, screen time, clicks, searches and browsing trajectories cease to be neutral residues and come to compose a diffuse production of behavioral signals that feeds profiling, segmentation and modulation of conduct, converting experience into raw material for valorization <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29; p. 66)</4>. At the dogmatic level, the point is not to equate the user with an employee, but to show that the enjoyment of the IOC occurs in an environment of opaque governance of the collection, processing and economic use of data, which prevents the consumer from auditing the correspondence between signs of “service”, “personalization” and “free of charge” and the real conditions of exploitation, updating factual vulnerability in its semiotic feature and straining duties of transparency and informational loyalty <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 66)</6>. <7>↩</7>

In Dowbor, capture oriented by retention and return metrics depends on an architecture that organizes the visible, the desirable and the probable, converting attention and behavior into an economic input at individualizable scale <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29-30)</2>. The author insists, however, on the ambivalence of the technological base, whose political materialization can either sustain forms of democratic connectivity or expand the capacity for corporate manipulation on a larger scale <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 39)</4>. The decisive hermeneutic point is that the relevant harm is not reduced to dispersed monetary costs: it may occur ex ante, in the intelligibility of the offer and in the shaping of the decision under interested curation, requiring that duties of information, transparency and loyalty be read in light of the consumer's perceptual integrity and of internal parameters of control of abusive teleologies. <5>↩</5>

“Functional isolation” designates the practical effect of the demand monopoly: the utility of the dominant service is inseparable from the fact that it concentrates the network and its links, so that exclusion (by blocking, banning, obsolescence or loss of account) is equivalent, in everyday life, to exclusion from circuits of work, social life and information, because the platform comes to operate as infrastructure of social participation. In this grammar, formally existing alternatives may be insufficient when they do not preserve functional equivalence (interoperability, migration of contacts, history, libraries and communication standards) and when exit implies a rupture of communicability itself; it is in this sense that “freedom of choice” loses material density, since choosing outside the standard may mean, in practice, not being able to communicate and not being able to belong. Gigantism, far from being a competitive accident, stems from technical characteristics that accelerate concentration and make domination rapidly planetary <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 24)</2>, converting standards into coercion. At the dogmatic level, the usefulness of the category is to show that signs such as “option”, “consent” and “available alternatives” may conceal structural dependence and unilateral governance of access, bearing on duties of loyalty, information and the prohibition of frustrating the purpose of consumption in the CDC; and, when control rights and private rules function as a power of social and symbolic exclusion over IOCs, the social function of property and of IP itself is placed back as an internal limit of legitimacy of this governance. <3>↩</3>

In a close critical key, it is relevant to note the expression enshittification, popularized by the Canadian Cory Doctorow <1>(2023)</1> to describe the process of progressive degradation of digital platforms that, after attracting and locking in users, come to reconfigure the experience to capture value from different groups dependent on the ecosystem, with deterioration of the utility originally offered. The expressive popularity of the expression in the anglophone digital environment <2>AMERICAN DIALECT SOCIETY</2><3>(American Dialect Society, 2024)</3> works as a symptomatic record of an internationally recognized phenomenon, consisting in the architectural degradation of enjoyment in digital environments after the consolidation of functional dependence on the platform. <4>↩</4>

Dowbor calls inflation from monopoly profits (profit-inflation) the macroeconomic effect of the pricing power exercised by private intermediation infrastructures when dominant standards and points of passage become unavoidable, so that the increase in fees and commissions comes to have repercussions as inflation without depending on classical demand pressures or cost shocks: “When these prices rise and impact inflation, they generate inflation from monopoly profits (profit-inflation).” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</2>. In this key, the rise in prices is compatible with a rentier rationality of maximizing dividends through markups defined by the structural position of the intermediary, draining income through subscriptions, fees and access “rights”, which explains the author's refusal of the conventional monetary diagnosis and his direct critique of the Central Bank's justifications: “It is not demand inflation, and the justifications of the Central Bank […] are simply false”. <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 70)</4>. <5>↩</5>
