The discussion on technofeudalism and digital rentierism then moves to the operational level from a central question about how it is possible for platforms to manage to extract value from ontologically non-scarce goods and, at the same time, to stabilize positions of power that analogically approach feudal lordship.

In the regime of IOCs, the business model tends to depend on a deliberate engineering of scarcity and risk, converting enjoyment into a toll circuit and permanence into a practical obligation. The platform does not profit only by “selling”, but by governing access, modulating the experience and making exit costly.

When technical reproduction is cheap and availability could be expanded, income is not sustained by natural rarity, but by produced rarefaction, which shifts the center of gravity of economic power. Instead of competing above all on productive efficiency or on the intrinsic quality of a good, what comes to matter is controlling gateways, protocols, <1>p. 209</1> interfaces, catalogs and authorization regimes, that is, controlling the very symbolic and technical infrastructure that organizes consumption.

In the immaterial domain, technical reproducibility lowers marginal cost and shifts the conflict to the control of access. For this reason, when persistent unavailability, exclusivity and “last chance” are observed, the decisive datum is not natural rarity, but rarefaction by design, sustained by regimes of authorization, catalog and visibility that transform abundance into toll.

In the domain of immaterial goods, subjection intensifies because technical reproduction dissolves the limit that traditionally contained economic power, which is physical rarity. In digital objects, the marginal cost of reproduction tends to fall drastically and, in theory, availability could expand without requiring productive capacity comparable to the factory, logistics and extraction of inputs. For this reason, when a persistent regime of unavailability, exclusivity and last chance is observed in these markets, one is not facing a natural condition of the object, but a deliberate institutional choice, so that scarcity appears not as fact, but as project.

The consequence is that the platform ceases to monetize only the delivery of a good and comes to monetize control of access and of time. It does not sell a “thing”, it sells passage, permanence and predictability in an environment governed by itself. And, for this government to generate income, friction must be reintroduced where technique would produce abundance. At this point, artificial scarcity and rentierism cease to be mere <1>marketing</1> and productivity tactics and become structural operators of the business model in operation itself.

The platform creates windows, rotations, <1>tiers</1>, seasonal events, passes, countdowns, limited bundles and mechanisms of conditioned acquisition. It then converts this arrangement into narrative, speaking of “rarity”, “exclusive”, “last chance”, “collectible” and “special edition”. This narrative, in turn, is operationalized by interfaces and rules that make the user's experience dependent on continuous attention. The non-scarce is transformed into the scarce by design and, in doing so, the basis of a rent economy is consolidated.

This regime of rarefaction by design finds, in the diagnosis of informational rentierism, its most direct economic translation. What is monetized is the authorization to enter, to remain, to accelerate, to distinguish oneself and not to lose. The platform, therefore, does not operate merely as a supply of goods, since it operates as the turnstile of an environment in which the consumer only preserves value if they accept cycles of repeated charging and moving terms. It is <1>p. 210</1> at this point that artificial scarcity ceases to be ornament and becomes engine, since it continuously manufactures the practical conditions for the toll to seem natural.

At the microarchitectural level, this appears clearly in continuous digital services, especially in the games-as-a-service ecosystem. Acquisition ceases to mean the stabilization of a good outside the supplier's reach and comes to mean enjoyment conditioned by governance. The consumer does not buy a “thing” and take it with them; they enter an access regime in which the object remains functional only within an infrastructure they do not control, crossed by updates, balancing, ends of events, catalog rotation, reconfigurations of internal currency and policy changes. The platform monetizes access in layers: it charges for entry, charges for acceleration, charges for convenience, charges for symbolic differentiation, charges for return and, above all, charges for the mitigation of the risk that it itself manufactures.

Thus, the informational rentierism described by Dowbor <1>(2024)</1> finds its microarchitectural correlate in the everyday life of platforms. The toll does not present itself only as an entry price. It reappears as repeated charging for permanence, organized around time, attention and the predictability of cycles. In the industrial economy, the consumer pays to acquire a good whose existence, once purchased, tends to stabilize outside the supplier's reach, at least within reasonable expectations of durability and of the discipline of quality defects.

The critical point is that this model needs its own grammar of risk. In classical markets, relevant risk is risk of quality defect, malfunction, insecurity, objective non-compliance with the offer. Here, the efficient risk is another: the risk of missing the <1>timing</1>, of missing the window, of losing status, of “falling behind”, of seeing symbolic value evaporate and, of course, the risk of losing functional value within the ecosystem. It is an engineering of opportunity and belonging, its consumer is not compelled by the lack of the good itself, but by the threat of discontinuity of their position within the environment.

This alters the legally relevant object of the relationship. Coercion does not appear as violence, nor as direct prohibition, nor as explicit imposition of purchase; it appears as functional and semiotic dependence, built by design. The platform governs scarcity in time, and by governing time it governs the economic meaning of the object. The value of what was “acquired” comes to depend on cycles, calendars, rotations and unilateral rules. Consumption, in this register, becomes the administration of anxiety. Its experience is organized so that continuous presence seems a rational requirement, and not a capture.

<1>p. 211</1> Having understood rentierism as a logic of recurring extraction, it remains to make explicit its operational mechanism in continuous enjoyment. Under the proposed hypothesis and empirical laboratory, extraction does not depend primarily on raising “upfront” prices, but on managing risk and scarcity as an architecture of conduct, producing an economy in which the consumer decides under time pressure, under threat of symbolic loss and under structural opacity as to the future of the catalog and the rules. The economic diagnosis then becomes a legal axis, since the platform does not merely offer, it governs, and governs by design.

The manufacture of risk is central to understanding why artificial scarcity is not a marketing detail, but a technique of power. In environments of continuous enjoyment, the most effective risk is not the risk of the product “not working”, which would correspond to a classical grammar of quality defect by inadequacy. The decisive risk is the risk of loss of opportunity, the risk of falling behind, the risk of not belonging, the risk of losing status, the risk of seeing the desired object go out of circulation and the risk of the symbolic identity built in the ecosystem suffering depreciation.

This risk is not natural. It is calibrated by the platform through a temporal architecture, with seasons, <1>splits</1>, <2>metas</2> and missions. It is also calibrated by an architecture of offer, with rotation, programmed exclusions and variable catalogs. Added to this is an architecture of reward, with progression systems and <3>grind</3>, and a sanctioning architecture, with bans, restrictions, automated penalties and opaque policies. The user finds themselves compelled to follow, to return and to keep up with the ecosystem, on pain of symbolic and material-digital loss.

The temporal architecture that manufactures urgency does not operate only through seasons and rotation, since it becomes discipline when the bond itself is formatted as a circuit of tasks. Missions are the operational name of this conversion. They bring consumption up against labor by transforming permanence into a requirement to “earn” what will later be presented as a reward or as a right to unlock. The command does not appear as an authoritarian order, but as an infantilized phrase of social contract: do something, receive something. In terms of political economy, it is the typical gesture of transforming time into currency without ever calling it labor, and of transforming engagement into value without ever calling it production <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2017d)</2><3><4>227</4></3>.

<1>p. 212</1> The contract does not leave this mechanism at the level of the rhetoric of “events” and “fun”. It incorporates it into the very grammar of acquisition of virtual goods by recording that access to Game Currency and to Virtual Content may occur by purchase, by receipt or by earning, and that this “earning” may come from completing missions or tasks. The platform, therefore, formally recognizes that there is a path of obtaining that does not pass through direct payment, but through the fulfillment of internal objectives, which are objectives defined by the supplier itself, with criteria and rewards defined by the supplier itself, and whose effectiveness depends on permanence in the ecosystem. This is not a detail. It is the moment at which the incorporated exterior, which seemed merely a “user”, is reconfigured as an operator who works to make enjoyment itself possible, stable and monetizable <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2024e)</3><4><5>228</5></4>.

When the mission becomes the unit of organization of time, what is bought and what is “earned” come to mix in the same circuit. Currency and item no longer appear as simple delivery, but as a prize conditioned on the fulfillment of an agenda. This agenda, in turn, produces the central effect that Marx describes in diffuse labor, since the consumer is induced to internalize as a need what is, ultimately, a requirement for the reproduction of command. The game becomes a metagame, and the metagame becomes a mechanism of extraction. The reward, instead of freeing the user, ties them to the cycle, since it presents itself as “progress” and “accumulation” that only make sense while the platform keeps alive its regimes of equivalence, visibility and distinction <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2017f)</2><3><4>229</4></3>.

For such a description not to become an abstraction, it suffices to observe that the ecosystem's own interface dictionary records missions as objectives with criteria, progress tracking and rewards, varying by events and seasons. The consumer, thus, does not merely play. They execute an agenda of production of numbers, presence and compliance, whose social form is that of an obligation disguised as choice. Diffuse productivity becomes routine. And routine becomes, without scandal, a method of monetization <1>League of Legends Wiki</1><2>(League of Legends Wiki, [202-?]f)</2>.

When this control over the existence and duration of the object is exercised systematically to intensify urgency, dependence and extraction, the problem ceases to be merely <1>p. 213</1> “contractual freedom” or a “legitimate business model” and becomes one of purpose. The rationality of the system reveals itself in the pattern, not in the episode. The dividing line does not lie in the fact that artificial scarcity exists, nor in the fact that the offer exploits rarity as a sales technique, but in the way scarcity and temporality are mobilized to produce, predictably, frustration of utility, lowering of adequacy or precarization of the functional and positional value that grounded the consumer's consent. If scarcity is produced as an instrument of recurring capture and if access is designed as precarious authorization, the architecture comes to operate against the legitimately expected functional minimum, straining good faith, material transparency and balance. In this framing, the discussion about clauses and policies is not peripheral. It is the visible surface of a teleology embedded in the design of the service. This prepares the dogmatic qualification of the deviation of purpose when the arrangement itself is calibrated to exploit the consumer's inability to audit the equivalence between promise and delivery.

This distinction can be visualized through the contrast between positional scarcity and corrosive scarcity. The sale of a commemorative edition or of a rare cosmetic item for a short window may manufacture urgency and capture value through opportunity, provided that it preserves intact the delivery owed and offers the consumer clear parameters on duration, form of access, limits of the offer and possible future repetition. This is additive rarity, whose effect falls on the consumer's choice without lowering the integrity of what has already been acquired nor degrading the experience of those who choose not to buy. Different is the design in which the object or the set of advantages already obtained deliberately lose status, power, practical relevance or use value if the consumer does not pay for new layers, does not fulfill retention routines or does not submit to imposed update cycles, manufacturing default by architecture. In this second scenario, scarcity ceases to be a simple commercial strategy and comes to operate as a mechanism of frustration of adequacy, because the maintenance of the functional value of the object is converted into a permanent toll, charged in money or in compulsory presence, which reconfigures the contract as a dynamic of unstable permission and reinforces, through the very structure of the design, the supplier's governance asymmetry.

There is, however, an even more commonplace and equally abusive mode, which does not depend on loss of access nor on extreme degradation of functionality, and which manifests itself as positional deception by omission. When the platform sells an item at a high price under the promise of exclusivity, or presents exclusivity as a relevant attribute to justify price and spending, it incorporates this quality into the content of the offer and into the perceived utility of the object. In these cases, the consumer does not pay only for aesthetics or immediate <1>p. 214</1> availability, but for the promised rarity, for the status and for the social distinction that the very symbolic architecture of the ecosystem enforces. If, after a period, the same item reappears in an alternative store, in special currency, in an aggressive promotion or at a significantly lower price, and if the temporal limitation of the exclusivity was not adequately and understandably informed at the time of acquisition, there is a retroactive reconfiguration of the value delivered, with frustration of legitimate expectation and violation of transparency. Scarcity, here, may operate as an expedient for capturing consent under informational inadequacy, with potential framing as misleading advertising by omission and non-compliance with the offer, in addition to breaking the equivalence between spending and utility delivered as legitimately expected. The legal consequence is not exhausted in subjective discomfort, since the subsequent change of the attribute that justified the price may call for material restoration through the typical means of consumer law, by refund, reduction or equivalent functional compensation, and may also open space for losses and damages when additional harm arising from the positional deception is demonstrated.

Artificial scarcity functions, then, as an economic operator and as a legal operator. At the economic level, it converts replicable goods into assets apt to sustain recurring monetization. At the legal level, it is frequently anchored in exclusivity rights and in contractual arrangements that authorize unilateral control of the catalog, of the rules and of the very ontological status of the object, such as revocable licenses, non-transferability and reservations of alteration, in addition to access and interface architectures that make enjoyment an unstable permission. The result is a form of market in which asymmetry is not limited to the supplier's “better knowledge”. It materializes in the supplier's very capacity to define what exists, for how long it exists, under what conditions it exists and under which narratives it exists, including as to positional attributes offered as components of the price. For this reason, artificial scarcity must be understood as part of an architectural teleology. It integrates a set of design choices oriented to extraction and not to the simple efficient organization of a naturally limited resource, and it is at this threshold that it ceases to be merely commercial strategy and becomes a legally relevant category for the qualification of the deviation of purpose when the equivalence between promise and delivery is made opaque or deliberately frustrated.

Architectural teleology does not manifest itself only in clauses and policies, but in the way the interface organizes visibility, calculation and risk. It is at this level that the toll becomes material, even if it does not take the form of explicit charging. Three traits tend to repeat. The first is the coercive time window, which shortens the space of decision and converts not acting <1>p. 215</1> into predictable loss. The second is the sanction for absence, in which the mere interruption of use triggers a lowering of status, access or opportunity, transforming permanence into a practical obligation. The third is the opacity of price and equivalence, obtained through intermediate currencies, bundles and conversions that prevent the consumer from comparing cost, measuring spending and auditing, in functional terms, the promise and the delivery. When these traits combine, the toll ceases to be a simple marketing strategy and becomes coercion incorporated into the mode of enjoyment.

A recurring example is the battle pass, in which the consumer pays for the possibility of unlocking items, but actual enjoyment depends on a race against time and on an imposed volume of engagement that, if not met, converts the initial payment into precarious access and projected loss. The urgency is not circumstantial. It is manufactured to push the consumer to devote disproportionate screen time, or to make a new purchase to compensate for the loss of pace, making non-use a designed form of default. Another example is the programmed lowering of ranking and visibility due to inactivity, which converts absence into punishment and makes anxiety a cost of maintaining position, even when there is no new functional delivery to justify the degradation. A third example is the system of layered virtual currencies, in which the purchase is not made in legal tender, but in intermediate credits and successive conversions that fragment perception, mask the real price and hinder comparison, reinforcing the inability to audit equivalence between what is promised and what is delivered. These mechanisms are not mere <1>design</1> adornments. They constitute the normal mode of charging the toll in continuous immaterial consumption.

The administration of this relationship, however, tends to take an even more characteristic form, which helps to understand why these mechanisms are so effective. The platform treats the consumer relationship itself as a game in itself, a metagame parallel to the main product. The user is there for the matches, for the interaction with others and for the competitive experience of the game, but, in the interface, is induced to take part in a continuous dispute for the maintenance of access, opportunity and status, now not against other players, but against the very structure that governs the environment. It is an unfair game by design, because the supplier is simultaneously referee, creator of the rules, manager of the scoreboard and beneficiary of the informational asymmetry. By converting permanence tasks, time windows and progression systems into the language of merit, the platform shifts to the consumer the burden of avoiding predictable losses and normalizes the idea that enjoyment depends on “making an effort” not to lose what has already been acquired or to preserve symbolic value within <1>p. 216</1> the ecosystem. The house always wins, not by rhetorical fatalism, but because the governance regime controls the conditions of victory, reconfigures goals, alters equivalences and administers scarcity, time and visibility as instruments of recurring extraction.

The legal relevance of these mechanisms stems from the fact that they reconfigure the consumer's decision-making autonomy and the very adequacy of the object, by shifting the center of value to conditions of enjoyment that are unstable, unilaterally administered and hardly transparent. Scarcity, in this context, is not only the rarity of the item, but the governed rarefaction of time, opportunity and recognition. When the platform designs the experience to produce predictable loss, impossible calculation and dependence on permanence, it transforms supply into a dynamic of unstable permission and reinforces the deviation of purpose already indicated, because the architecture comes to operate against the legitimately expected utility and against the trust that sustained the contracting.

It is from this point that the category of the IOC becomes absolutely necessary to guarantee intelligibility for the consumer user. In continuous digital services, the immaterial object of consumption is not an isolated good. It is a bundle of functions and signs whose integrity depends on coherence between promise, delivery and preservation of value over time. When the platform organizes artificial scarcity and risk as pillars of the business model, it shifts consumption to a regime of enjoyment in which the consumer's autonomy is systematically strained by urgencies, by opacities and by identity dependence. The consumer decides under produced conditions. This is not merely informational vulnerability. It is semiotic and temporal factual vulnerability, since the field of choice is pre-formatted and the economic meaning of the object depends on the very environment the supplier governs.

In this framework, the IOC functions as an operator for reconstructing supply and for controlling the supplier's justificatory discourse. It obliges one to treat as legally relevant variables that, on platforms, tend to be precisely the variables of extraction. Among them are the durability of functional value, the minimum stability of the conditions of enjoyment, the governance of the catalog, the reasonable predictability of changes and the possibility of auditing what was promised as utility.

If the ecosystem is structured to produce risk, scarcity and dependence as engines of consumption, legal analysis cannot remain restricted to the episodic reading of a term nor to the snapshot of a <1>patch</1>. What is qualified is a regime of governed enjoyment. It is this permanence of the mechanism that allows moving from economic description to the identification of <2>p. 217</2> an operative purpose and, where applicable, to the characterization of the unlawful act of abusive teleology.

When the decisive risk becomes the risk of loss of opportunity and position, the platform gains an instrument of command that does not depend on the isolated quality of a product. The axis ceases to be “delivering something” and becomes “retaining someone”. The discipline is not “buy this”; it is “remain accessible”, “be present”, “follow the cycle”, “don't miss the window”, on pain of devaluation of what has been accumulated up to then. The coercion is soft, but structuring, since it appears as a rationality of permanence.

It is here that the metaphor of technofeudalism leaves the aesthetic plane and takes on the role of functional description. Power is not stabilized only by price, but by exit cost. Leaving means abandoning history, reputation, library, items, progression, affective investments, networks of sociability and, in certain cases, the very capacity to take part in communities that organize themselves within that ecosystem. The more the object of consumption is governed enjoyment and not a delivered thing, the more the dependence is on infrastructure, and the more “competition” becomes a dispute over entrapment by <1>design</1>, not over the excellence of the good.

Continuous extraction is not sustained only by recurring charging, since it depends on a return of value that comes not in the form of price, but in the form of activity. Each session, click, match, search, comment, purchase, withdrawal, return and comparison keeps the ecosystem alive and feeds metrics, network effects, reputations, hierarchies and engagement cycles. This is more than measurement, because this activity is converted into data and metrics, processed by telemetry and by machine learning models that refine monetization strategies, calibrate reward probabilities and modulate matchmaking and recommendation algorithms, adjusting the very functional architecture of the Immaterial Object of Consumption.

The platform is not merely selling experience, since it converts presence into an asset, which is worth as much economically, in revenue, <1>valuation</1> and market power, as politically, in the capacity to influence conduct and to structure meanings. The user continuously tests, legitimizes and improves the system, providing behavioral <2>feedback</2> on a massive scale, without any legal recognition of this diffuse labor.

The institutionalization of the Public Beta Environment (<1>Public Beta Environment</1>, <2>PBE</2>) makes this diffuse labor visible in its most literal form. The ecosystem creates a “downstairs” of experimentation, in which the collectivity is summoned to test future versions, to live with instability, to report failures and to expose, at scale, behaviors that function as a dress rehearsal of what will be launched in the main environment. What presents itself <3>p. 218</3> as an opportunity to “help” and “test new features” is, in practice, the material incorporation of the consumer into the productive process, not as final recipient, but as a piece of calibration. The user, here, is not only measured, they are mobilized as a distributed workforce that reduces the cost of quality control, expands the surface of bug detection and feeds the supplier's organizational intelligence, producing a productivity that does not appear as labor, but as participation <4>Riot Games</4><5>(Riot Games, 2024j)</5><6><7>230</7></6>.

This incorporation can be read more precisely when one observes how the contract treats the informational core of this same circuit. In the Unsolicited Idea Submission Policy, the supplier declares that it “values” <1>feedback</1>, but simultaneously structures the regime of appropriation, by reserving for itself the free use of ideas, suggestions and creative materials sent by the user, without this generating economic consideration, compensation or a duty of recognition. The effect, at the Marxian level of the incorporated exterior, is transparent. The user's contribution is useful, is absorbed and comes to compose the metabolism of the ecosystem, but it is legally “dehydrated” so as not to become credit, remuneration or a bond. The <2>PBE</2> laboratory, then, is not merely a testing space, since it functions as an institutional symbol of what the contract does in silence. The platform admits and administers diffuse productivity, but preserves the asymmetry of command, converting collaboration into an appropriable input <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4><5><6>231</6></5>.

So as not to turn this description into an innocuous metaphor, it should be noted that the PBE is not described as a “parallel” server for ordinary enjoyment. It is presented as a testing environment oriented to future features and, therefore, as a stage of quality adjustment prior to “live”. The very existence of a stabilized and continuous public testing infrastructure indicates that the ecosystem needs this incorporated exterior to maintain the update cycle without paying the corresponding cost in internal labor. What appears, to the consumer, as a privilege of early access, appears, to the social form of the arrangement, as a machine for extracting time, attention and technical reporting in exchange for a promise of belonging <1>League of Legends Wiki</1><2>(League of Legends Wiki, [202-?]g)</2>

This productivity is diffuse, but organizable, because the platform captures data on use and attention and also captures social proof, diffusion and symbolic validation. This includes content <1>p. 219</1> generated by the user themselves, such as posts, comments, streams, memes, guides and reviews, which becomes an engine of visibility and recommendation and functions, in practice, as invisible labor of production and marketing of the IOC. What circulates in this environment is not only money, but also status, belonging, visibility, comparison and distinction, so that the value of the IOC does not reside only in the object, but in the social and semiotic environment that surrounds it.

Among the most ostensive forms of this invisible labor is the work of content creators, <1>streamers</1> and influencers who orbit the ecosystem as if they were autonomous “microentrepreneurs”, when, in practice, they function as an intense public face of the incorporated exterior. The platform benefits from a mass of communicational labor that not only talks about the game, but translates the game, explains the game, gives intelligibility to the catalog and sustains the collective desire that keeps symbolic rarefaction operative. This is the production of meaning as infrastructure. In the platform rent economy, producing meaning is producing value, because the consumer only pays for distinction when distinction is recognized and when this recognition is socially produced.

This ambiguity is reinforced by the contractual design itself. On the one hand, the contract insists that use is “personal” and “non-commercial”, pushing creative work into a zone of conditioned tolerance, dependent on authorization, exceptions or a specific program. On the other hand, the company maintains institutional support channels for creators, with partnership programs and benefits, formalizing a functional integration without converting this integration into an employment bond nor into duties equivalent to those of an employer <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025m)</2><3><4>232</4></3>. In this combination, the platform captures the creator's diffuse productivity as advertising and as a living informational manual of the ecosystem, but maintains the asymmetry of command, because the creator's permanence, access to benefits and the very possibility of monetizing content depend on private, revocable and selective rules.

The capture becomes even clearer when one observes the problem of intelligibility of the cosmetic “product”. As of the date of conclusion of this research, the <1>client</1><2><3>233</3></2> does not offer, in the purchase flow itself, a robust and generalized preview mechanism that <4>p. 220</4> allows the user to audit the experience of a <5>skin</5> before acquiring it, so that the decision depends, to a relevant extent, on external mediations that display, compare and describe the content. Riot's own representatives publicly acknowledge this discomfort when announcing experiments with mechanisms for offering previews of <6>skins</6>, making explicit that the user often does not know precisely what they are acquiring at the time of purchase <7>RIOTMIKOUZ</7><8>(RiotMikouz, 2025)</8><9><10>234</10></9>. In this void, channels such as <11>SkinSpotlights</11> come to function, in practice, as prostheses of the ecosystem's duty to inform, because they display what the consumer cannot audit within the normal purchase circuit <12>SKINSPOTLIGHTS</12><13>(SkinSpotlights, 2026)</13><14><15>235</15></14>. The result is that a formally external agent is incorporated as a necessary piece of the circulation apparatus, delivering intelligibility, reducing the risk of regret and sustaining the consumer's practical trust in the purchase, without receiving any legal status corresponding to the economic function it performs within the regime<16><17>236</17></16>.

In this picture, the user contributes to manufacturing the very rarity that governs them, since, in the immaterial, rarity is not substance, but grammar. Whoever defines this grammar, that is, what counts as legendary, exclusive, <1>meta</1> or essential, controls the circuit of value. Artificial scarcity produces urgency of purchase and also urgency of presence, because, for the narrative to be sustained, the crowd needs to see, dispute, comment and desire. Without an active community, rarity loses effectiveness. Thus, the consumer of the IOC is not only a consumer, since they are, structurally, also an input.

With this, the notion of incorporated exterior<1><2>237</2></1> gains a decisive layer of intelligibility. The user not only pays and produces, but also legitimizes and patrols, <3>p. 221</3> sustaining the value of the environment through presence and sustaining the governability of the environment through collective performance and defense of the fief. Recurring extraction depends, therefore, on a design that simultaneously organizes cheap symbolic rewards, material costs internalized by the consumer and visibility mechanisms capable of improvising an audience and suppressing frictions. Artificial scarcity, in this picture, is not only rarefaction of supply. It is rarefaction of recognition, of opportunity and of belonging, administered to convert community into gear, engagement into value and loyalty into an exit barrier. This architecture confirms the thesis that capture is not a marketing accident, but architectural teleology, because the mechanism reproduces itself precisely by transforming mediated life into a requirement for the functioning of the rent regime.

At this moment, with a strictly functional scope and without pretension of exegetical reconstruction, it is justified to draw, by strict structural homology, on the figure of the lumpenproletariat as presented by Karl Marx<1><2>238</2></1>. The objective is not to transpose categories of the employment relationship to digital consumption, nor to shift the framing of the consumer microsystem to a general theory of class struggle. The term is employed as a key of intelligibility for an analogous power structure, in which subjects situated outside regular formal production are functionally incorporated into a regime of valorization, and can be mobilized as a mass of support, legitimation and stabilization of a command, including under the appearance of spontaneity, leisure and “community participation”.

In the platform environment, this homology describes a specific mechanism of functional incorporation of the consumer. The user's presence, permanence, performance, sociability and collective recognition operate as infrastructure of network value and symbolic value. Positional goods and regimes of administered scarcity depend on this social base to convert rarity into prestige and prestige into price. It is not a matter of asserting an employment bond, but of identifying an unpaid social co-production of value, captured and converted into revenue through unilateral governance of the rules, of visibility, of the catalog and of the conditions of enjoyment. In dogmatic terms, this datum does not change the nature <1>p. 222</1> of the relationship as consumption. It qualifies the governance asymmetry and reinforces the centrality of duties of material transparency, loyalty and protection of trust in continuous adhesion contracts, precisely because the supplier administers, without real auditability by the consumer, the parameters that define what is worth, what appears and what is considered “rare”.

It is also in this key that a decisive and recurring practical element in digital consumption is understood, which the language of the lumpenproletariat helps to illuminate without reducing the phenomenon to a sociological identity. The platform not only captures the user's participation as an economic condition of the ecosystem. It can mobilize it as a technology of stabilization of command. Consumers become activist defenders of the very regime that captures them, patrolling discourse, imposing community norms, harassing criticism and naturalizing tolls and reconfigurations of equivalence as if they were merit, “deservingness” or simple individual choice. This mobilization effect is not accessory, because it functions as a layer of legitimation and of social <1>enforcement</1> of the <2>design</2>, increasing the practical opacity of the system and hindering collective reaction, which deepens and exacerbates the position of vulnerability and makes it even more relevant to delimit dogmatically when the architecture frustrates adequacy, transparency and trust, converting participation into an instrument of extraction.

Historically, this is a layer situated at the margins of regular productive labor, unstable and heterogeneous<1><2>239</2></1>, whose relevance, in the Marxian analysis, does not lie in being a “producing class” in the industrial sense, but in occupying a social position of exteriority to the classical circuit of labor that, even so, can be functional to certain arrangements of power. The parallel that matters here is neither identitarian nor historical, but structural.

<1>p. 223</1> The consumer-user of platforms finds themselves formally outside the wage relationship and outside the classical categories of labor that sustained industrial dogmatics, but they are materially incorporated into the regime of valorization as a constant source of diffuse productivity and as the base of support of the toll.

From this point of view, the consumer approaches a digital lumpenproletariat: they participate intensely in the production of value, but do so on an opaque plane, outside the traditional categories of labor, employment contract or provision of services. Their exploitation occurs not only through the extraction of direct income, but through the structural capture of their subjectivity (of their symbolic identity and of their personal integrity) as raw material for the mode of production. When progress, status, reputation and the very continuity of access to the Immaterial Object of Consumption become dependent on unilateral decisions of the platform, the consumer finds themselves in a position analogous to that of the worker subjected to living conditions defined by others, but without the law recognizing them as such.

This is an external agent who, instead of being irrelevant, is converted into an economic gear precisely because it does not present itself as labor, but as mediated life, attention, circulation and conduct. This homology helps to clarify a decisive characteristic of digital rentierism. Extraction by platform does not depend only on selling goods or services. It depends on governing a set of social behaviors converted into economic matter. The platform captures the user's time, but also captures their insertion in the collective, with visibility, comparison, distinction, belonging and reputation. This capture is simultaneously economic and semiotic.

The platform needs the user to be there, returning, circulating and feeding the ecosystem because it is from this return that the data, the network effects and the very valuation of the environment are manufactured. The “cloud serf” produces without a contract, without a wage and without recognition as labor. And it is precisely there that the effectiveness of the regime lies. Extraction is naturalized as entertainment, as habit, as sociability and as a consumer micro-decision.

The technofeudal specificity of the arrangement appears even more forcefully when one observes the inversion of infrastructure costs. In industrial capitalism, the holder of capital provides machines, facilities and means of production, subordinating labor through material control of the productive apparatus. In the regime of IOCs, the consumer comes to finance, with their own resources, the minimum infrastructure of their own economic and semiotic incorporation, paying for <1>hardware</1>, electricity and connectivity in order to remain in an environment that converts their presence into someone else's asset. This is a functional mutation of <2>p. 224</2> command, since the formally external subject not only feeds the system with data and attention, but also internalizes the material cost of maintaining the access that enables the capture. The result is a model in which extraction rests on a prior investment by the exploited themselves, naturalized as a technical condition of participation and masked as a consumer choice.
